'''''Pittosporum undulatum''''' is a fast-growing tree in the family [[Pittosporaceae]]. It is sometimes also known as '''sweet pittosporum''', '''native daphne''', '''Australian cheesewood''', '''Victorian box''' or '''mock orange'''.

''Pittosporum undulatum'' has become invasive in parts of Australia where it is not indigenous. It is also highly invasive in [[South Africa]], the [[Caribbean]], [[Hawaii]], the [[Azores]] and southern [[Brazil]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.angra.uac.pt/PESSOAIS/DOCENTES/jbatista/Projectos/Projectos.pdf |title=''Pittosporum undulatum'' in southern Brazil |publisher=Instituto Hórus |access-date=18 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081023233725/http://www.angra.uac.pt/pessoais/DOCENTES/JBatista/Projectos/Projectos.pdf |archive-date=23 October 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.angra.uac.pt/PESSOAIS/DOCENTES/jbatista/Projectos/Projectos.pdf |title=''Pittosporum undulatum'' in the Azores, Portugal |publisher=Universidade dos Açores |access-date=18 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081023233725/http://www.angra.uac.pt/pessoais/DOCENTES/JBatista/Projectos/Projectos.pdf |archive-date=23 October 2008}}</ref>

==Description==
''Pittosporum undulatum'' grows as a shrub or small tree to {{cvt|15|m|ft}} tall.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Pittosporum~undulatum |title=''Pittosporum undulatum'' |website=PlantNET |author=New South Wales Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust |date=2000}}</ref> Its evergreen leaves are lance-shaped (lanceolate), with wavy (undulating) margins. It carries conspicuous orange woody [[fruit]]s about 1 cm in diameter for several months after flowering in spring or early summer.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hear.org/Pier/wra/pacific/pittosporum_undulatum_htmlwra.htm |title=''Pittosporum undulatum'' |website=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk |date=5 February 2005 |access-date=22 March 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090329022009/http://www.hear.org/pier/wra/pacific/pittosporum_undulatum_htmlwra.htm |archive-date=29 March 2009}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
French botanist [[Étienne Pierre Ventenat]] described ''Pittosporum undulatum'' in 1802.

==Distribution and habitat==
Originally ''P.'' ''undulatum'' grew in moist areas on the [[Australia]]n east coast, where its natural range was from south-east [[Queensland]] to eastern [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]],<ref name=Gleadow>{{cite journal |last1=Gleadow |first1=Ros |last2=Walker |first2=Jeff |title=The invasion of Pittosporum undulatum in the Dandenong Ranges, Victoria: realising predictions about rates and impact |journal=Proceedings: Fifth Victorian Weeds Conference |date=May 2014 |url=https://www.academia.edu/22464521|access-date=10 May 2016}}</ref> but has increased its range since European settlement.

==Ecology==
Likely pollinators of its flowers are moths and butterflies, as the flower produces a fragrant perfume at night. The fruit are eaten by [[Currawong|currawongs]], [[Red-whiskered bulbul|red-whiskered bulbuls]], [[Indian mynah|Indian mynahs]] and [[Grey-headed flying fox|grey-headed flying foxes]]. Seed is dispersed in bird faeces.<ref name=Benson2000>{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Doug |last2=McDougall |first2=Lyn |year=1999 |title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 7a: Dicotyledon families Nyctaginaceae to Primulaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=402–508 [462] |url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/RoyalBotanicGarden/media/RBG/Science/Cunninghamia/Volume%206%20-%201999/Volume-6(2)-1999-Cun6Ben402-509.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313135801/https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/RoyalBotanicGarden/media/RBG/Science/Cunninghamia/Volume%206%20-%201999/Volume-6%282%29-1999-Cun6Ben402-509.pdf |archive-date=13 March 2016}}</ref>

This species is attacked by a range of herbivorous insects. Larvae of pittosporum longicorn (''[[Strongylurus thoracicus]]'') bore into sapwood, pittosporum beetle (''[[Lamprolina aeneipennis]]'') consumes leaves, two fly species form leaf galls (''[[Phytoliriomyza pittosporophylli]]'') and twig galls (''[[Phytoliriomyza pittosporocaulis|P. pittosporocaulis]]''), pittosporum psyllid (''[[Trioza vitreoradiata]]'') forms small lumps on leaves, gall thrips (''[[Teuchothrips]]'' spp.) often infest leaves, while pittosporum bug (''[[Pseudapines geminata]]'') and several [[scale insect]] species feed on the sap.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rojas-Sandoval |first=J |date=2015-04-13 |title=Pittosporum undulatum (Australian cheesewood) |journal=CABI Compendium |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=45705 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.45705|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Path to Poço da Alagoinha, Flores, Azores, Portugal (PPL3-Altered) 3 julesvernex2.jpg|thumb|''Pittosporum undulatum'' forests on the Azores]]

According to the [[Australasian Virtual Herbarium]], the earliest-known record of ''P. undulatum'' is from [[Port Jackson]], Sydney, in 1803.<ref name=Gleadow/> However, its status around the [[Sydney]] area is contentious.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uow.edu.au/science/biol/esa/posters/howell.pdf |title=''Pittosporum undulatum''{{snd}}Traitor or Survivor? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070916025247/http://www.uow.edu.au/science/biol/esa/posters/howell.pdf |archive-date=16 September 2007}}</ref> Even though it is native to the region, it has spread to soils and bushland where it wasn't found before European settlement, often out-competing other plants.

''Pittosporum undulatum'' is the most invasive tree species in the [[Azores]], and has spread through most of the mid- to low-altitude forests, out-shading and replacing native trees, such as ''[[Myrica faya]]'' and ''[[Laurus azorica]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pittosporum undulatum Vent. |url=https://acores.flora-on.pt/#1Pittosporum+undulatum |publisher=[[Flora-On]] |access-date=9 December 2021}}</ref>

It has done especially well in areas where the environment has been altered by humans – for example by [[habitat fragmentation]] weakening other natives or due to [[fertilizer]] runoff from homes increasing soil nutrients. Unlike most natives, it takes advantage of high nutrient levels and its seeds can germinate without needing fire. That has led to the species sometimes receiving the "invasive" label, although some{{Who?|date=January 2012}} think that it is merely returning to areas where it grew before people arrived in Australia and began burning the environment far beyond that which previously occurred.{{Citation needed|date=June 2009}}

Recommended control measures have included the identification and selective removal of female trees to prevent spread, as well as careful burning, where possible, together with follow-up weeding.<ref name=Gleadow/>
